sentences.text: The name Pliosaurus means "more lizard" because the animal's appearance was considered more reminiscent of crocodilians than of other plesiosaurs. Pliosaurus belongs to the large-headed, short-necked "pliosauromorph" morphotype, unlike the small-headed, long-necked "plesiosauromorph" morphotype. Pliosaurus had massive, short cervical vertebrae with flattened, subcircular to oval centers.
P. kevani is the only recognized Pliosaurus species with sub-trihedral teeth, featuring slightly flattened labial surfaces and finely distributed enamel ridges.

The second known specimen of P. funkei was famously nicknamed "Predator X" before its formal description. Due to their remarkable size, the teams nicknamed the holotype of P. funkei "The Monster" and the referred specimen "Predator X". Before formal description, media estimates suggested P. funkei reached 13 to 15 meters and the P. kevani holotype reached 12 to 16 meters.
P. funkei gained media attention leading to its appearance in a 2009 History Channel documentary and a 2010 science fiction horror film.
The name P. kevani honors Kevan Sheehan, a cafe owner who collected most of the holotype skull during his daily walks along the shore.
P. kevani is notable for having a large postcranial skeleton, which is rare for the genus.

The genus Pliosaurus was formally described by Richard Owen in 1841. Although mentioned in 1824, Pliosaurus was not formally described until 1841 by Richard Owen, who first placed it in Plesiosaurus before elevating it to its own genus later that year.
In 1824, William Daniel Conybeare established the species Plesiosaurus giganteus for plesiosaur specimens with shortened cervical vertebrae.

Plesiosaurs likely maintained a constant body temperature, possibly through endothermy, similar to birds. A 2019 study suggests Plesiosaurs had enlarged red blood cells that aided them during diving. Pliosaurus is considered a visually oriented predator with greatly enlarged orbits indicating high visual acuity. Unlike modern whales, Plesiosaurs did not possess echolocation due to a lack of acoustic isolation in their auditory capsules.

Pliosaurus was a top marine predator with an exceptionally strong bite, though its skull was weak against twisting forces. Unlike relatives adapted to small prey, Pliosaurus favored a strategy of short, targeted bites to the back of the jaw where pressure was greatest. Pliosaurus exerted a bite force of 9,600 to 48,000 newtons, comparable to or greater than the largest living crocodilians.

Pliosaurus skulls were reinforced to withstand the stresses of feeding. The rostrum of some Pliosaurus species likely contained a neurovascular system capable of detecting prey movements in the water.

A specimen of P. carpenteri showed advanced degeneration of the jaw joint that caused the lower jaw to misalign progressively. Pathological features in a P. carpenteri specimen included bone growth around tooth sockets and irregular cavities in the jawbone.
As a top predator, P. funkei likely ate other marine reptiles found in its environment. Pliosaurus were giant predators that ate fish, squid, and other marine reptiles.

Phylogenetic studies place Pliosaurus in a derived position within Thalassophonea, often showing it is related to Gallardosaurus. Benson and colleagues identified six valid species of Pliosaurus in 2013: P. brachydeirus, P. rossicus, P. funkei, P. kevani, P. westburyensis, and P. carpenteri. Harry Govier Seeley established the family Pliosauridae in 1874 to include animals similar to Pliosaurus.

Pliosaurus fossils date from the Late Jurassic to the Lower Cretaceous, specifically from the Kimmeridgian to the Valanginian stages, with a possible record from the Oxfordian stage. Pliosaurus lived from the Upper Jurassic to the Lower Cretaceous in what is now Europe and South America. Due to their remarkable size, the teams nicknamed the holotype of P. funkei "The Monster" and the referred specimen "Predator X".

Several species of Pliosaurus lived during the Upper Jurassic in the Kimmeridge Clay Formation of England. Based on the distribution pattern of pliosaurs, it is believed they had a cosmopolitan distribution, similar to modern whales.

Knutsen and colleagues suggest that P. funkei and P. rossicus might represent different growth stages of the same species, though they maintain them as distinct taxa. Benson and colleagues argue that the differences between P. westburyensis and P. carpenteri are significant enough to warrant separate species status.
